newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India-Pakistan talks to resume despite missile row.
newsitem.headline: India-Pakistan talks to resume despite missile row.

text.p: India and Pakistan are set to resume peace talks on Thursday despite tensions over a reported movement of Indian missiles towards the Pakistani border.
Both sides seem keen not to let their fragile dialogue be sabotaged by the row over new Prithvi missiles India is said to have moved to within 100 km (60 miles) of the border.
"We don't think it will be a factor at all in the talks," said a diplomatic source in New Delhi. "It has added one more point which they (the Pakistanis) will raise and we will reply.
"We have our own concerns, namely the proxy war in Kashmir. That remains our main concern. We want to see evidence that Pakistan is reducing aid to such people (militants)," he said.
Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms, trains and finances separatist guerrillas fighting since 1990 to end Indian rule over the two-thirds of Kashmir under Delhi's control.
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry spokesman, Khalid Salim, said Islamabad did not intend to focus too much on the missile row.
"This is an issue that is bound to come up, but we are not making it into a big issue in the talks because we have much more complicated and important issues to discuss," he said.
He said it was too early to say if any progress could be made on the long-running Kashmir dispute, which has bedevilled previous attempts to reconcile the South Asian rivals.
Islamabad wants Kashmiris to be allowed to vote whether to join Hindu-majority India or Islamic Pakistan, while India says the Himalayan region is an integral part of its territory.
Salim said Pakistan was hoping for the best ahead of this week's talks, which are a follow-up to ice-breaking meetings at the same level held in New Delhi at the end of March.

The foreign ministers of the two countries met in Delhi in April and Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif held talks in a cordial atmosphere with his Indian counterpart Inder Kumar Gujral at a regional summit in the Maldives last month.
"We on our side are going into it (the talks) with an open mind and with all kinds of expectations," Salim said.
"Our ultimate aim is normalisation and cooperative relations. For that we want to set the procedure in motion and then it can move under its own steam," he said.
Both foreign ministries say the talks will aim to set up joint working groups to tackle the issues dividing India and Pakistan, but details are not yet clear.

Some Pakistani analysts fear the positive chemistry achieved in the Maldives might be upset by what are perceived here as provocative Indian actions -- an alleged violation of Pakistani airspace by an Indian MiG-25, the killing of a Pakistani officer in cross-border firing and the alleged Prithvi movement.

India has denied the alleged airspace violation and says border shooting incidents are common. Gujral has denied the medium-range Prithvis had been deployed, without commenting on reports they had been moved to storage in Jullundur.

"In my opinion these incidents may unfortunately upstage whatever progress had earlier been achieved at (the Maldives capital) Male," said Ghani Jaffar, researcher at the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies.
He said Sharif's letter to the permanent members of the U.N. Security Council asking them to restrain India from posing a missile threat showed how seriously Pakistan took the issue.

Fahmida Riaz, senior research associate at Islamabad's Institute of Strategic Studies, said she expected no major breakthroughs to emerge this week, but it was important that the two antagonists were maintaining their dialogue.
"In the present state of relations, I am only optimistic about these talks in the sense that we do not have a communication gap. At least we are exchanging views," she said.
She said the two sides might discuss key issues such as Kashmir and their high-altitude military standoff on the Siachen Glacier, but were unlikely to make rapid progress.
For Islamabad, progress on the Kashmir dispute is vital if advances are to be made on economic, cultural and other fronts, but neither side has shown any sign of changing its position.

"We want to raise the profile of economic relations, people-to-people contacts," said the diplomatic source in New Delhi. "When tensions (in Kashmir) are low, it will be possible to be creative and adventuresome. But we have to end the war."
